en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 56.1 (SN 56.1, PTS SN v 414) 1. Samādhivagga Samādhisutta: Concentration At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when concentration by mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness. When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. When the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. “What, bhikkhus, is concentration by mindfulness of breathing? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing rapture, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing rapture, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing pleasure, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing pleasure, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the mental formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the mental formation, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the mind, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the mind, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Gladdening the mind, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Gladdening the mind, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Concentrating the mind, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Concentrating the mind, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Liberating the mind, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Liberating the mind, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Contemplating fading away, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating fading away, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Contemplating cessation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating cessation, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out. This, bhikkhus, is called concentration by mindfulness of breathing. And how, bhikkhus, is it that concentration by mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness? Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu breathes in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or whenever he breathes out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long’—on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world. Whenever a bhikkhu breathes in short… [as above] …he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out’—on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that concentration by mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness. And how, bhikkhus, do the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment? Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, on that occasion unmuddled mindfulness is established in him. Whenever unmuddled mindfulness is established in a bhikkhu, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused by the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of mindfulness goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, on that occasion he is ardent, not lax. Whenever a bhikkhu is ardent, not lax, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of energy is aroused by the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of energy; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of energy goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, on that occasion there is awareness in him of what is inside and outside. Whenever there is awareness in a bhikkhu of what is inside and outside, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of discrimination of states is aroused by the bhikkhu;

on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of discrimination of states; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of discrimination of states goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, on that occasion he is neither constricted in mind nor distracted externally. Whenever a bhikkhu is neither constricted in mind nor distracted externally, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of rapture is aroused by the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of rapture; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of rapture goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, on that occasion his mind is not unconcentrated. Whenever a bhikkhu’s mind is not unconcentrated, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of concentration is aroused by the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of concentration; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of concentration goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, on that occasion he does not neglect wisdom. Whenever a bhikkhu does not neglect wisdom, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused by the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity; on that occasion the enlightenment factor of equanimity goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. And how, bhikkhus, do the seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation? Whenever, bhikkhus, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused in a bhikkhu, and he develops it, and makes much of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is developed in him, and it goes to fulfillment by development. Whenever, bhikkhus, the enlightenment factor of energy is aroused in a bhikkhu, and he develops it, and makes much of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of energy is developed in him, and it goes to fulfillment by development. Whenever, bhikkhus, the enlightenment factor of discrimination of states is aroused in a bhikkhu, and he develops it, and makes much of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of discrimination of states is developed in him, and it goes to fulfillment by development. Whenever, bhikkhus, the enlightenment factor of rapture is aroused in a bhikkhu, and he develops it, and makes much of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of rapture is developed in him, and it goes to fulfillment by development. Whenever, bhikkhus, the enlightenment factor of concentration is aroused in a bhikkhu, and he develops it, and makes much of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of concentration is developed in him, and it goes to fulfillment by development. Whenever, bhikkhus, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused in a bhikkhu, and he develops it, and makes much of it, on that occasion the enlightenment factor of equanimity is developed in him, and it goes to fulfillment by development. Whenever, bhikkhus, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and made much of, on that occasion true knowledge and liberation are developed in him, and they go to fulfillment by development. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that the seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

“Monks, a monk who is concentrated understands things as they really are.
And what does he understand as it really is?
He understands: ‘This is suffering’ as it really is; he understands: ‘This is the origin of suffering’ as it really is.”
‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ he understands it as it really is; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ he understands it as it really is.
Monks, develop concentration.
“Monks, a monk who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.

Therefore, monks, the application of effort should be made thus: ‘This is suffering,’ the application of effort should be made; ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ the application of effort should be made;
‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ the application of effort should be made; ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ the application of effort should be made.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 56.2 (SN 56.2, PTS SN v 414) 1.
The Chapter on Concentration (Samādhivagga)
The Discourse on Seclusion:
“Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to seclusion.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is secluded understands things as they truly are.”
And what does one understand as it really is?
One understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; one understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’;
one understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; one understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
One understands it as it truly is.
"Monks, apply yourselves to seclusion.
A monk who is secluded, monks, understands things as they truly are."

"Therefore, monks, the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus: ‘This is suffering’; the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus:
‘This is the cessation of suffering’; the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.3 (SN 56.3, PTS SN v 415) 1. Samādhivagga First Discourse on the Son of Good Family At Sāvatthī. “Monks, when a son of good family possesses four qualities, he is one who has entered upon the way leading to the complete destruction of suffering. What four? Here, monks, a son of good family possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped at, leading to concentration. When a son of good family possesses these four qualities, monks, he is one who has entered upon the way leading to the complete destruction of suffering.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever sons of noble family have in the past rightly gone forth from the home life into homelessness, all of them did so for the sake of the direct realization of the four noble truths as they really are.

Bhikkhus, whatever sons of noble family will in the future rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, all of them will do so for the sake of the direct realization of the four noble truths as they really are.”
"Monks, whatever sons of good family at present go forth from the home life into homelessness, all do so for the sake of the realization, as it truly is, of the Four Noble Truths.
Of which four?

Of the noble truth of suffering, of the noble truth of the origin of suffering, of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and of the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
"Monks, whatever sons of noble family in the past went forth from the home life into homelessness rightly...
[and] will go forth...
[and] are now going forth—all of them do so for the sake of the realization, as it truly is, of these four noble truths."

"Therefore, monks, the application of mindfulness should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’; the application of mindfulness should be made thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; the application of mindfulness should be made thus:
‘This is the cessation of suffering’; the application of mindfulness should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. This is the third [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.4 (SN 56.4, PTS SN v 415) 1. Samādhivagga The Second Discourse on the Son of Good Family “Monks, there are these five powers of a noble son. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of a noble son. When, monks, a noble son possesses these five powers, he is capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna, even in this very life.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever sons of noble family in the past rightly went forth from the home life into homelessness and realized things as they truly are, all of them realized the four noble truths as they truly are.

Bhikkhus, whatever sons of noble family in the future will rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness and realize things as they truly are, all of them will realize the four noble truths as they truly are.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever sons of good family at present have rightly gone forth from the home life into homelessness and realize things as they truly are, they all realize the four noble truths as they truly are. What four?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
"Whatever sons of noble family, monks, in the past, rightly went forth from the home life into homelessness and realized things as they truly are...
[and those who will realize them]...
[and those who are realizing them], all of them realize these four noble truths as they truly are."
"Therefore, monks, the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.5 (SN 56.5, PTS SN v 416)
1. The Chapter on Concentration (Samādhivagga) The First Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Bhikkhus,
whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have fully awakened to reality as it truly is, they all fully awakened to the four noble truths as they truly are.
"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will fully awaken to things as they truly are, all of them will fully awaken to the four noble truths as they truly are.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present are fully awakening to things as they truly are, all of them are fully awakening to the four noble truths as they truly are.
Which four?"
The noble truth of suffering …pe… the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, in the past have fully awakened to these as they really are …pe… will fully awaken to them …pe… [all have done so by means of this very path].
“Those who fully awaken—all of them fully awaken to these four noble truths as they really are.
Therefore, monks, the application of effort should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’ … [as before] … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
The fifth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 56.6 (SN 56.6, PTS SN v 417) 1. Samādhivagga The Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘ascetic, ascetic. In what way, venerable sir, is one called an ascetic? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu has abandoned the five hindrances, those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one is called an ascetic. “But, venerable sir, it is said, ‘brahmin, brahmin. In what way, venerable sir, is one called a brahmin? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu possesses the four bases for spiritual power. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one is called a brahmin. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir, how well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith... and the power of wisdom. Now, venerable sir, in what way is the power of faith fulfilled? And in what way is the power of energy fulfilled? And in what way is the power of mindfulness fulfilled? And in what way is the power of concentration fulfilled? And in what way is the power of wisdom fulfilled? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.

This, Ānanda, is called the power of faith. And how, Ānanda, is the power of energy fulfilled? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, possessed of firmness and persistence, not shirking the burden of wholesome states. This, Ānanda, is called the power of energy. And how, Ānanda, is the power of mindfulness fulfilled? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses mindfulness and alertness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago. This, Ānanda, is called the power of mindfulness. And how, Ānanda, is the power of concentration fulfilled? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple, withdrawn from sensual pleasures, withdrawn from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of withdrawal. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and contains purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, Ānanda, is called the power of concentration. And how, Ānanda, is the power of wisdom fulfilled? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses wisdom; he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the power of wisdom. In this way, Ānanda, the power of faith is fulfilled; in this way the power of energy is fulfilled; in this way the power of mindfulness is fulfilled; in this way the power of concentration is fulfilled; in this way the power of wisdom is fulfilled.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past proclaimed what they had fully awakened to as it really is, all of them proclaimed the four noble truths as they had fully awakened to them as they really are.

Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will proclaim what they have fully awakened to as it really is, all of them will proclaim the four noble truths as they have fully awakened to them as they really are.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins at present proclaim what has been fully awakened to as it really is, all of them proclaim the four noble truths as they have been fully awakened to as they really are.
Which four?
The noble truth of suffering … [and so on] … the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
"Monks, whatever recluses or brahmins in the past have proclaimed what has been fully awakened to as it really is...
[and] will proclaim...
[and] do proclaim, all of them proclaim these four noble truths as they have been fully awakened to as they really are."
"Therefore, bhikkhus, the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.7 (SN 56.7, PTS SN v 417)
1. The Chapter on Concentration (Samādhivagga) The Discourse on Thoughts (Vitakkasutta):
“Monks, do not give rise to evil, unwholesome thoughts, such as these:”
Sensual thought, thought of ill will, and thought of cruelty.

And why is that? Because, monks, these thoughts do not lead to what is beneficial, nor to the fundamentals of the holy life; they do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.
And while reflecting, monks, you should reflect: "This is suffering"; you should reflect: "This is the origin of suffering"; you should reflect:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; you should reflect: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
For what reason?

“Monks, these thoughts are connected with the goal; they pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life; they lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.

Therefore, monks, an effort should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’... [and so on] ...an effort should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.8 (SN 56.8, PTS SN v 418) 1. Samādhivagga Cintasutta “Bhikkhus, when one thing is cultivated and made much of, unarisen defilements do not arise and arisen defilements are abandoned. What is that one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body. When this one thing, bhikkhus, is cultivated and made much of, unarisen defilements do not arise and arisen defilements are abandoned.”
“Monks, do not harbor an evil, unwholesome thought such as:
‘The world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’; ‘the world is finite’ or ‘the world is infinite’;
‘the soul and the body are the same’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’; or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death’...”

“Or: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
And for what reason? Because...”

“Monks, that reflection is not connected with the goal, it does not pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life, and it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
But when you reflect, monks, you should reflect: ‘This is suffering’; you should reflect: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; you should reflect:
‘This is the cessation of suffering’; you should reflect: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”
For what reason?

Because, monks, this reflection is connected with the goal; it pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life; it leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
Therefore, monks, the application of effort should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”
The Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 56.9 (SN 56.9, PTS SN v 419) 1.
The Chapter on Concentration (Samādhivagga)
The Discourse on Controversial Talk: “Monks, do not engage in controversial talk, saying:
‘You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. What do you know about this?’”
"You do not understand the Dhamma and Vinaya. You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. What is consistent for me is inconsistent for you.
You said later what should have been said earlier, and said earlier what should have been said later.
Your position has been overturned. Your argument has been refuted; go and seek deliverance from that argument. You are defeated; try to extricate yourself if you can."
For what reason?

Because, monks, that talk is not connected with the goal, it does not pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life, and it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
And when you speak, monks, you should say: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering."
"You should say, 'This is the cessation of suffering'; you should say, 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering'...
[and so on] ...a yoga should be practiced.
The ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 56.10 (SN 56.10, PTS SN v 419) 1.
Samādhivagga Tiracchānakathāsutta (The Discourse on Animal Talk)
“Monks, do not engage in various kinds of worldly talk,
such as: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks,
talk of clothing, talk of bedding, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles;”
Talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about the countryside, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells,
talk about departed ancestors, talk about various matters, talk about speculations concerning the world, talk about speculations concerning the ocean,
or talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be."
For what reason?

Because, monks, that talk is not connected with the goal, it does not pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life, and it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
And when you speak, monks, you should say: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering."
"You should speak thus: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; you should speak thus: 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
For what reason?

Because, monks, this discourse is connected with the goal, it pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life, and it leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna."
"Therefore, monks, the application of mindfulness should be practiced thus: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
(The tenth.
The First Chapter on Concentration is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Concentration, seclusion,
and two other sons of noble family.
"Monks and brahmins [speak of] thought,
reflection, and contentious talk.

2. The Chapter on Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dhamma:
The Discourse on Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
“Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth.
Which two?”
“Monks, this devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—and this devotion to self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial:

not approaching either of these two extremes, monks, the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, it produces knowledge, and it leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to Nibbāna.”
And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to Nibbāna?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"This, monks, is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
And what, monks, is this Noble Truth of Suffering?
Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering..."

Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with what is disliked is suffering, separation from what is liked is suffering, not to obtain what one desires is also suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
And this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering:
That which is this craving, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
that is to say, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
And this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
The complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, and non-attachment:

this, monks, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—that is, this very Noble Eightfold Path; namely: [the right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration].
“Right view … right concentration.
‘This is the noble truth of suffering,’ monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
‘That this noble truth of suffering must be fully understood,’ monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me vision … light.”
“‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me, monks, vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me, monks, vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.”
"Furthermore, monks, regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering as something to be abandoned: before my time...

The Discourse on the Aggregates:
“Monks, there are these four noble truths. Which four?”
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering?
It should be said: "The five aggregates of clinging," namely—
The aggregate of clinging to form …pe… the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
That craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—
that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks,
is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its abandonment, its release,
and non-attachment to it— this, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very noble eightfold path; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
"This, monks, is called the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
These, monks, are the four noble truths.
Therefore, monks, an effort should be made to understand: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … an effort should be made to understand: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’"

The First Discourse on Koṭigāma.

“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating four noble truths that we have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time—both I and you.

both you and I. It is through not awakening to and not penetrating the noble truth of the origin of suffering … [and] the noble truth of the cessation of suffering …”
Because of the non-awakening and non-penetration of the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, this long course has been run and this long journey traversed by both you and me.
But now, monks, that noble truth of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; that noble truth of the origin of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated;
that noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; [and] that noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering...

“Because of not seeing the Four Noble Truths as they really are;”
For a long, extended period of time,

The conduit to existence has been uprooted;
the root of suffering is severed;
now there is no further becoming.

and those venerable ones do not, even in this very life, attain the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood.

There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Once upon a time, monks, a certain man left Rājagaha thinking,

“Bhikkhus, that man saw the fourfold army entering the lotus stalks on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond.

‘I am indeed mad; I am indeed deranged.’”
‘What does not exist in the world has been seen by me.
Then, monks, that man, having entered the city, announced to the great multitude of people:
‘Venerable sirs, I am indeed mad; venerable sirs, I am indeed deranged.’”
‘What does not exist in the world has been seen by me.
‘But how, good man, are you insane? How have you lost your mind?
And what is it that does not exist in the world which has been seen by you?’”

“Here, Bhante, having departed from Rājagaha with the thought, ‘I shall reflect on worldly matters,’ I approached the Sumāgadhā lotus pond. Having approached, I sat down on the bank of the Sumāgadhā lotus pond, reflecting on worldly matters.

"And there is nothing in this world that has been seen by me.
"Truly, good man, you are mad; truly, you have lost your mind.
There is nothing in this world that has been seen by you."
Moreover, monks, that man saw what was real, not what was unreal.
Once in the past, monks, a battle between the devas and the asuras had been arrayed.

"Defeated, monks, the asuras, terrified, entered the city of the asuras by way of the lotus-root tunnel, seeking to delude the gods themselves.
Therefore, monks, do not concern yourselves with worldly thoughts, such as:
'The world is eternal' or 'the world is not eternal,' or 'the world is finite' or 'the world is infinite.'"
“‘The soul is the same as the body,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’;

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Come, monks, let us go to Paṭibhānakūṭa for our midday rest.
“Very well, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a large number of monks, went to Paṭibhānakūṭa.
A certain bhikkhu saw a great precipice at Paṭibhānakūṭa.
Having seen it, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this is indeed a great precipice; venerable sir, this precipice is truly terrifying.”
“Venerable sir, is there another precipice more vast and more terrifying than this one?
“There is, bhikkhu, another precipice more vast and more terrifying than this one.
“But what, venerable sir, is that other precipice more vast and more terrifying than this one?”
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; do not understand as it really is:

They delight in volitional formations that lead to birth; they delight in volitional formations that lead to aging;
they delight in volitional formations that lead to death; they delight in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Delighting in those volitional formations that lead to birth, delighting in those volitional formations that lead to aging,
delighting in those volitional formations that lead to death, and delighting in those volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair,

They form volitional formations; they form volitional formations that lead to death; they form volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Having formed volitional formations that lead to birth, and having formed volitional formations that lead to aging...
Having performed volitional formations that lead to death, and having performed volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair,
they fall into the abyss of birth, they fall into the abyss of aging,
they fall into the abyss of death, and they fall into the abyss of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They are not fully released from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

But as for those recluses or brahmins, monks, who understand "this is suffering" as it really is... [and so on].
Those who understand, as it truly is, ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ do not delight in volitional formations that lead to birth;
they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to aging; they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to death;
they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Being disenchanted with volitional formations that lead to birth, disenchanted with volitional formations that lead to aging,
disenchanted with volitional formations that lead to death, and disenchanted with volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair,
they do not form even those volitional formations that lead to birth, nor even those that lead to aging.
They do not form volitional formations; they do not form volitional formations that lead to death; they do not form volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Having not formed volitional formations that lead to birth, and having not formed volitional formations that lead to aging, they...

Without forming volitional formations that lead to death, and without forming volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, they do not fall into the abyss of birth;
they do not fall into the abyss of aging; they do not fall into the abyss of death;
and they do not fall into the abyss of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They are completely liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"They are completely liberated from suffering," I say.

Therefore, monks, the application of effort should be made thus: "This is suffering"... [and so on] "...this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus, monks, the application of effort should be made.

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms.

The Venerable Ānanda saw many Licchavi youths practicing archery in the assembly hall; even from a distance, through a small opening in the palm-leaf screen, they were shooting arrows one after another without missing the mark.
Having seen this, it occurred to him:
"Truly well-trained are these Licchavi youths; truly well-disciplined are these Licchavi youths!"
"For indeed, they will strike their arrows one after another without fail, from a great distance through a fine palm-leaf opening. Then,
having walked for alms in Vesālī and returned from his almsround after the meal,
the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Vesālī for alms.
There, Bhante, I saw many Licchavi youths practicing archery in the assembly hall; from a distance, through a small keyhole, they were shooting arrows one after another without missing the mark.”
Having seen this, it occurred to me:
"Truly well-trained are these Licchavi youths, truly well-disciplined are these Licchavi youths;
for how they, from afar, shall shoot arrows through a fine keyhole one after another without missing!"
“What do you think, Ānanda,
which would be more difficult to do or more difficult to achieve: one who, from afar,
with a fine palm-leaf arrow, should shoot an arrow after another in continuous succession without missing, or one who should pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with the tip [of another hair]?”

The Third Subsection on the Simile of Raw Grain: The Discourse on Gold and Silver “Bhikkhus, there are these five obstructions, hindrances, encumbrances of the mind that weaken wisdom. What five? Sensual desire is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom. Ill will is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom. Sloth and torpor are an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom. Restlessness and remorse are an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom. Doubt is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five obstructions, hindrances, encumbrances of the mind that weaken wisdom. Just as, bhikkhus, when raw grain is stored in a granary, it becomes an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance to the people; so too, these five obstructions, hindrances, encumbrances of the mind weaken wisdom. So too, bhikkhus, there are these five obstructions, hindrances, encumbrances of the mind that weaken wisdom. What five? Sensual desire... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five obstructions, hindrances, encumbrances of the mind that weaken wisdom. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will abandon sensual desire, which is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom; we will abandon ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... doubt, which is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encumbrance of the mind that weakens wisdom. Because, monks, the four noble truths have not been seen. Which four?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
